body_text: If you need to build business apps without writing code, Softr and Glide are two of the most talked-about no code platforms on the market right now. But they solve different problems for different teams. This detailed comparison of softr vs glide breaks down exactly where each tool fits, where it falls short, and when you should look at alternatives like Jet Admin for more demanding scenarios. Key Takeaways When you softr compare against Glide, the decision comes down to your primary use case, data architecture, and how much control you need over permissions and governance. Both are capable no code builders with ai features, drag and drop interface design, and free plan options, but they target different workflows. Softr is generally better for web-based client portals, partner portals, membership sites, and multi-role business apps connected to multiple data sources. Softr is ideal for client and partner portals where external users need filtered access to their own records. Glide is stronger for polished, mobile first apps and internal tools built quickly from spreadsheets or glide tables. Glide excels at creating fast, mobile-focused internal applications for field teams and operational workflows. Both platforms share a similar no code DNA with intuitive building blocks and AI-powered app development, but they differ significantly in data model: Softr is built for external business data across many sources, while Glide centers on Glide Tables and spreadsheet-style data with row-based limits. Both have free plans, usage and record limits, and web-only deployment (no true native app store binaries) as of mid-2026. Your decision should hinge on data sources, permissions, and app complexity rather than surface-level marketing about mobile vs web. For teams that outgrow the limits of either platform-especially around governance, security, and connecting to existing databases- Jet Admin offers a more enterprise-ready path for building secure business apps and customer portals. Softr vs Glide: Quick Verdict and Side-by-Side Summary Here is the short answer: choose Softr if you need web applications like client portals, partner dashboards, or multi-entity business apps sitting on top of existing business data across tools like Airtable, Notion, or sql databases. Choose Glide if you need mobile-friendly internal tools built straight from google sheets or Glide Tables with strong built-in logic and a polished mobile user interface. Both enable users to ship custom apps fast, but they optimize for different outcomes. Category Softr (July 2026) Glide (July 2026) Best for Client portals, partner dashboards, web apps Mobile first design internal tools, field apps Typical buyer CS/ops teams, agencies, IT teams Small teams, field ops, spreadsheet power users Data model 17+ external sources + Softr Databases Glide Tables, Big Tables, Google Sheets Pricing posture Predictable record/user limits per plan Row-based tiers with update quotas AI capabilities AI Co-Builder for multi-page apps; embedded AI assistants AI for data extraction, app scaffolding, image/doc processing Deployment Web apps, PWA on higher tiers Web apps, mobile-optimized PWA Free plan Published app included, 1,000 records Cannot publish apps; build/test only A team building an agency client portal with invoices, documents, and per-customer data views would lean toward Softr. A team needing a field-tech inspection app or inventory check-in tool on phones would lean toward Glide, which is optimized for quickly building mobile-first apps. TL;DR: Choose Softr if your app idea centers on external-facing portals, desktop dashboards, or apps requiring data from many systems. Choose Glide if you need a mobile first design app built fast from spreadsheet data for an internal team. Consider Jet Admin if you need deeper governance, dozens of production data source connections, or stricter security. What Softr and Glide Are (and Who Uses Them) Softr and Glide are both no code platforms that let teams build web apps and business apps without traditional app development or coding knowledge. They share the goal of speed and abstraction: get a working app in front of users fast, without a technical background in software engineering. Softr positions itself as a web-first, AI-native builder for client portals, membership sites, internal tools, and dashboards powered by existing business data. Softr is commonly used for internal tools and dashboards by operations teams, agencies, and customer success managers who need to surface data from tools their organization already uses. Softr offers a visual builder with drag-and-drop blocks for assembling pages and workflows. Glide is a mobile-first platform that creates internal applications from spreadsheets and its own built-in database layer. Glide apps are popular with small teams, field workers, and non technical teams who want to turn a Google Sheet into a usable app in hours. Glide is recognized for fast app development and excellent mobile experiences. Common audiences for both include operations managers building self-service tools, customer success teams creating client portals, IT teams prototyping data driven applications, and agencies delivering custom solutions for clients. Neither platform gives you full control over backend infrastructure the way a custom stack would. They prioritize speed and accessibility over low-level customization, which matters for complex enterprise app development. When teams need secure customer portals or internal tools with deeper governance, granular permissions, and many production data sources, platforms like Jet Admin fill that gap. Use Cases: Client Portals, Internal Tools, and Mobile Apps Softr and Glide overlap in the no code space, but they lean toward different flagship use cases. Understanding where each tool shines-and where it struggles-saves you from hitting painful walls months into a project. Softr's strengths center on web-based client portals and membership-style apps. You get login areas, dashboards, content libraries, invoice and document blocks, stat widgets, and per-record filtering that shows each customer only their own data. If you need a partner portal where vendors log in and see their orders, documents, and status updates, Softr gives you the blocks and permissions to build that quickly. Glide excels at mobile first apps for internal teams. Field technician checklists, job dispatch apps, basic CRM on phones, inventory loggers, and simple employee self-service tools-these are the sweet spot. Glide is tailored for internal operational apps and mobile users, and the experience on a phone feels native and polished. Glide works best when your team already lives in spreadsheets and needs a clean front-end fast. There are clear limitations on both sides. Softr's mobile experience is secondary; desktop is where portals look best. Glide's desktop layouts can feel constrained for complex multi-column business dashboards compared with Softr's page builder. Choose by use case: Client portals and partner portals → Softr advantage Internal mobile tools and quick spreadsheet apps → Glide advantage Mixed web + complex workflows with many entities → consider Softr or a more robust tool like Jet Admin depending on governance needs Building Model and UX: How You Actually Build Apps Both Softr and Glide use a drag and drop interface for app development, but the mental model and level of flexibility differ day-to-day. How you think about building-pages vs screens, blocks vs components-affects speed and what you can create. Softr uses a page-and-block model. You assemble full pages (dashboard, account, billing) from pre built templates and blocks such as tables, forms, charts, hero sections, and lists. Each block is configured through panels rather than freeform pixel-level design. Softr's block-based design allows for visually compelling web pages, especially for portal layouts and branded dashboards. Softr supports more complex apps while remaining approachable for users at various skill levels. Glide uses a screen-and-component model. Each screen ties directly to a data source (a table, sheet, or relation) with components like lists, tiles, buttons, and detail views. The builder feels like configuring a mobile app UI with a strong data binding layer. Glide is optimized for mobile-first apps with a simple interface, and this data-first mental model clicks fast for spreadsheet power users. On the AI front: Softr's AI Co-Builder can scaffold a multi-page business app from a text prompt, acting as an ai app builder for non technical teams. Glide offers AI features for extracting data from documents, enriching records, and suggesting app structures or logic-useful for turning an app idea into something functional quickly. The trade-off: Softr tends to be faster for classic portal layouts but less customizable than full design tools. Glide's components feel polished but can box you into certain layouts, especially when you try to build unconventional web experiences. Data Layer and Integrations: Business Data, Data Sources, and Limits The biggest practical difference between softr and glide is how they treat data. This single factor often determines which platform is viable for your project. Softr connects to multiple data sources -over 17, including Airtable, Google Sheets, SmartSuite, HubSpot, Notion, sql databases, and its own Softr Databases (launched mid-2025). Softr supports over 17 data sources for richer app logic, and its data handling includes integration with HubSpot and Notion alongside other tools. Softr allows building apps on existing business data, meaning your single source of truth can stay where it already lives. Softr apps can utilize Softr Databases for data management when you want native performance-roughly 50 requests/second versus 3–5 for many external backends. Softr connects natively to 17+ data sources for scalability without requiring you to replicate or mirror business data into a new store. Glide primarily supports Google Sheets and Glide Tables as its core data source. Glide Tables (standard and Big Tables for larger datasets) are central to performance and advanced logic. Glide works best with Glide Tables and spreadsheets, and while it does support connectors for Airtable, Excel, and selected SQL databases, data is often centralized into Glide itself. On Glide's Enterprise tier , Big Tables support up to 10 million rows, but spreadsheet-source row limits are much lower (often around 25,000 rows per app). For business apps, this means: Softr is attractive if your single source of truth must remain in tools like Airtable, Notion, or SQL. Glide is attractive if you're comfortable moving or mirroring key datasets into Glide Tables. For teams that need to connect directly to dozens of production data sources (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, Stripe, HubSpot, Salesforce, and more) without replication, Jet Admin's integrations catalog covers over 50 sources natively. Customization and UX Design Options Both tools are opinionated about design to keep apps consistent, but Softr offers greater design flexibility for web applications compared to Glide. That said, each makes deliberate trade-offs. Softr's web-first customization includes sections, hero areas, lists, and portal-specific blocks that can be re-ordered and styled. Softr offers customizable layouts and navigation options, with theming controls for fonts, colors, and spacing suitable for branded client portal and membership experiences. You won't replicate a fully custom marketing site, but for portals and dashboards you have real design freedom. Softr is easy to use but has limited design options compared to full front-end frameworks-a fair trade for speed. Glide provides limited design customization compared to Softr, but this constraint is intentional: modern mobile-style cards, lists, and detail screens are fast to configure and hard to visually break. Glide's design is less customizable but speeds up development, which is exactly what you want when shipping an internal tool in a day. For advanced customization options, Softr supports custom code or vibe code for bespoke UI blocks, while Glide leans into custom actions and computed columns that affect behavior more than layout. Neither replaces a full front-end framework, but both cover most internal tool and portal needs. Branded, desktop-optimized portals and dashboards → Softr On-phone usability and quick "app-like" feel → Glide Authentication, Permissions, and Client Portal Security For serious client portals and business apps, login, user roles, and data access rules often matter more than UI styling. This is where the softr vs glide comparison gets consequential. Softr's authentication model includes built-in login and signup flows with support for multiple user groups and per-record user filtering. Each external user sees only their own records, making it practical for agency client portals, partner portals, and customer self-service dashboards. Softr enables users to set custom user groups and apply permissions at the page, block, record, and field level. Softr also offers "Ask AI" assistants embedded in apps that query live data while respecting these permissions. Glide's user permissions are role-based, suitable for internal teams. App users are typically mapped to rows in a "Users" table or to authenticated email addresses, with conditions controlling which screens and rows they can see. This approach is powerful for internal tools but may require more careful manual configuration for complex multi-tenant portals with many external users. Both tools offer evolving authentication options-email/password, magic links, social/OAuth in some tiers. Teams with strict SSO/SAML or SCIM requirements should verify latest vendor documentation, as these features typically appear only on enterprise plans for both platforms. When governance becomes critical, Jet Admin emphasizes secure customer portals and internal tools with role-based access at the row, column, and action level , plus support for modern auth providers (OIDC, Auth0, Google OAuth, Supabase Auth, and more) and branded custom domain experiences. Collaboration, Development Workflow, and Auditability As apps move from side projects to team-critical tools, collaboration features and change tracking become more important than pure building speed. In Softr, multiple editors can work in the same app workspace. Softr includes built-in workflows triggered by user actions and supports UI-triggered actions for workflow automation. Softr's visual workflow builder is AI-assisted for easier setup, which helps non technical teams automate processes without deep configuration. Version history and app history are available, with more retention on higher tiers. In Glide, shared workspaces and team plans support multiple builders iterating quickly. However, Glide offers limited workflow automation capabilities compared to Softr. Glide's automations can be complex to configure, especially for multi-step processes or conditional logic. Both platforms support integration with automation tools like Zapier and Make, and both extend functionality through third party services. But neither is a full enterprise DevOps platform. Audit logs, change tracking, and formal version control are limited compared to what regulated environments typically require. For teams with stronger governance needs, Jet Admin combines automations, permissions, connected data, and audit logs in a way that supports formal business workflows. Validating any platform's logging and access-review capabilities before committing is essential. Deployment, Hosting, and Production Readiness Both Softr and Glide are fully hosted SaaS no code platforms. You build in the browser and deploy to web URLs, with options for a custom domain on paid plans. Softr primarily produces web apps and portals accessible via desktop and mobile browsers. It can publish Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) on higher tiers-useful for mobile access-but does not produce true native iOS/Android binaries for the Apple App Store or Google Play as of mid-2026. Softr removes softr branding on paid plans, giving published app experiences a more professional look. Glide also deploys web apps, often with mobile-optimized interfaces. Glide apps run in the browser, can be installed as PWAs, but are not compiled as native store mobile apps without third-party wrappers. Despite the mobile first design marketing, glide apps are still fundamentally web applications. Production-readiness considerations include uptime expectations, dependence on the vendor's infrastructure, and constraints on exporting or self-hosting the full stack. If your organization needs on-premise or private-cloud deployment, data residency controls, or strict networking rules, neither Softr nor Glide offers that level of infrastructure control today. If your company requires strict hosting control, confirm current deployment options directly with vendors. Platforms that explicitly support self-hosting or deeper infrastructure configuration may be necessary for heavily regulated scenarios. Pricing Models, Free Plans, and Scalability Costs (2026) Pricing is dynamic. Always verify current pages for Softr and Glide before committing. Here is an anchored snapshot as of mid-2026. Softr's free plan includes unlimited apps, unlimited collaborators, a custom domain, and up to 1,000 records per database (5,000 total). Ten app users are included. The Basic plan starts at $49/month with up to 50,000 records per app for standard sources. Softr's Pro plan starts at $139 per month and includes 100 users and 500K records-a significant step up for growing portals. Business-tier apps scale to roughly 1 million records. Softr's pricing model provides predictable user and record limits compared to Glide, and Softr has no extra charges for external data syncing. Softr includes higher user and record limits on every plan relative to comparable Glide tiers. Glide's free plan is useful for learning but cannot publish apps-it is strictly for building and testing. Paid plans start with Explorer and Maker tiers ($19–$60/month), then Glide's Business plan starts at $199 per month with roughly 30 users, ~100,000 rows per app for high-scale sources, and ~5,000 updates/month. Glide's plans limit data record rows with additional charges for overages, and external data sources consume update quotas. Glide's update limits can make scaling unpredictable, especially for apps that grow data over time. The practical impact: as your app scales and accumulates years of historical business data, record limits and priced add-ons drive long-term total cost of ownership. Compare not just monthly list prices but also user counts, record growth, integrations, automations, and the operational risk of hitting limits. Some teams choose platforms like Jet Admin when they need to build internal tools on top of existing databases without copying data or paying per-row surcharges. Choosing Between Softr, Glide, and Alternatives for Business Apps Both Softr and Glide are capable no code builders. Your decision should follow your primary use case, data strategy, and security requirements-not platform marketing alone. Choose Softr if you are building client portals or partner portals, you want to sit on top of Airtable, Notion, or SQL without migrating data, external users and per-record permissions are core requirements, and you value desktop web UX for dashboards and membership-style layouts. Softr offers more features for teams that need to build web apps with native integrations across an extensive ecosystem of other tools. Choose Glide if you prioritize fast delivery of mobile-friendly internal tools, are comfortable modeling data in Glide Tables or spreadsheets, and can live within Glide's row-based limits. Glide is optimized for quickly building mobile-first apps where the learning curve is minimal for spreadsheet-savvy teams. Look beyond these two when you need to plug into dozens of production data sources without replication, enforce fine-grained roles across rows, columns, and actions, or build customer portals with stricter security and governance expectations. Review Jet Admin's customer-portal capabilities and integrations page as a next step for evaluating three platforms side by side. Start by testing both Softr and Glide's free plans. Document your must-haves: data sources, permissions, and audit needs. If you find yourself needing more advanced features around governance and direct database access, evaluate platforms like Jet Admin in parallel. The best tool is the one that matches your data reality, not the one with the best landing page. FAQ: Softr vs Glide for Business and Client Portals These FAQs cover edge cases and decision details not fully explored in the sections above. Is Softr or Glide better for secure client portals? Softr is generally stronger for classic client portals-dashboards, invoices, documents, per-customer data views-thanks to portal-focused blocks and granular record filtering. Glide can power simpler external apps but is more often used for internal tooling. For regulated environments or strict SSO/SAML needs, verify each vendor's current security and authentication capabilities as of your evaluation date. Jet Admin focuses specifically on secure customer portals built on top of existing databases and SaaS APIs; review Jet Admin's customer-portal page for more detail. Can Softr or Glide replace custom app development? Both platforms can replace many simple-to-moderately-complex apps-CRMs, inventory tools, basic client portals-especially where speed matters more than deep customization. They are less suitable when you need full control over backend logic and infrastructure, on-premise deployment, complex domain-specific algorithms, or extensive offline support. Treat Softr and Glide as excellent accelerators or MVP platforms and consider migrating to custom or more enterprise-grade solutions if constraints become critical as your app scales. How do Glide and Softr use AI features? Both platforms integrate AI into app building and data workflows, but with different emphases. Softr's AI Co-Builder generates full business app scaffolds from text prompts, and embedded "Ask AI" assistants let users query live app data while respecting permissions. Glide's AI features focus on extracting data from files, enriching records, and suggesting app structures or logic. AI capabilities are evolving rapidly-experiment during free trials instead of relying on static feature lists. Which platform is easier for non-technical teams to learn? Both are accessible to non-developers. Softr's page-and-block model often feels more familiar to people used to website builders, while Glide's data-first builder may click faster for spreadsheet power users. The learning curve depends more on your team's mental model (page-centric vs data-centric) than on tutorial availability-both have strong documentation and communities. Pilot both tools for a week with the same simple app (a basic client portal or internal directory) and see which mindset fits your organization. What if my business data lives in many different systems? This is where evaluating the data layer is crucial. Softr can connect to multiple data sources-Airtable, Notion, SQL, HubSpot, and more-keeping data live in its original location. Glide encourages centralizing data into Glide Tables with selected external connectors, which means syncing or copying. Map all critical data sources (databases, SaaS tools, spreadsheets) and check each platform's native connectors and sync patterns. If you prefer to build powerful custom apps directly on top of existing databases, warehouses, and APIs without replication, exploring platforms like Jet Admin-which supports over 50 data sources including other platforms and extensive ecosystems of connectors-may better fit your long-term architecture.

title: Ontop vs Deel: Which Global Payroll Platform Wins?
summary: Ontop vs Deel and the best Deel alternatives for paying global contractors: features, pricing, and why Ontop wins for cost-efficient global payroll.
body_text: If you are comparing Ontop vs Deel, you are really asking a bigger question: what is the best platform to hire and pay a global team, and which Deel alternative actually fits your business? Both handle global payroll, contractors, and EOR, but they are built for different kinds of company. Ontop is a global payroll and payments platform that lets companies hire and pay teams in 150+ countries, with built-in financial tools for the workers themselves. This guide compares Ontop and Deel on coverage, payments, compliance, and price, and shows where each one, and the main Deel alternatives, make the most sense. At a Glance: Ontop vs. Deel Comparison Feature Ontop Deel Core Focus Specialized in hiring, onboarding, and paying global teams efficiently. All-in-one HR platform for global teams. Best For Startups, SMBs, and contractor-heavy teams, especially in Latin America. Large enterprises needing a full suite of HR tools and broad EOR coverage. EOR Coverage Uses a partner-led model for global reach. Owns over 150 legal entities for direct EOR services. Contractor Payments Starts at $49 per contractor per month. Starts at $49 per contractor per month. Employee Payments Starts at $499 per employee per month. Starts at $599 per employee per month. Key Strength Cost-efficiency, streamlined experience, and built-in financial services for workers. Comprehensive HRIS, extensive integrations, and wide EOR entity network. Key takeaways Deel is a broad all-in-one HR suite; Ontop is a focused, lower-cost platform for hiring, paying, and giving workers financial tools, and is strong in Latin America. Contractor pricing is the same on both ($49 per contractor per month); Ontop's EOR starts lower ($499 vs $599 per employee per month). The best Deel alternative depends on the need: Ontop for cost-efficiency and worker payments, Remote and Rippling for enterprise HR breadth, Oyster and Multiplier for EOR coverage. The best platform to pay global contractors is the one that pays in full, on time, in a currency the worker controls, not the one with the most features. Ontop pays workers in USD into an Ontop Global Account they control, with the Ontop Visa Platinum Card to spend. What are the best Deel alternatives for international contractors? The best Deel alternatives for international contractors are platforms that pay contractors compliantly across borders without Deel's enterprise price or complexity. Ontop leads for cost-efficiency and worker-side financial tools, especially in Latin America. Remote and Rippling suit companies that want a full HR suite, while Oyster and Multiplier compete mainly on EOR coverage. Ontop: best for cost-efficient contractor and global payroll with built-in worker payments. Remote: broad EOR and HR for enterprises. Rippling: HR, IT, and finance in one, for larger teams. Oyster and Multiplier: EOR-focused coverage across many countries. Core Service Offerings Understanding the fundamental approach of each platform is key. Ontop and Deel solve global employment challenges but with different philosophies. Ontop: Focused on Hiring and Payments Ontop is built to make hiring, onboarding, and paying international workers seamless and cost-efficient. The platform is available in over 150 countries and specializes in providing the core tools businesses need to scale without unnecessary complexity. Key services include: Global Payroll: Automate payments to contractors and employees worldwide. Contractor Management: Hire and pay contractors with compliant, localized agreements. Employer of Record (EOR): Hire full-time employees in countries where you don't have a legal entity, with compliance handled for you. Built-in Financial Services: Workers gain access to the Ontop Global Account and the Ontop Visa Platinum Card, adding flexibility and optimizing their compensation. Deel: A Comprehensive HR Suite Deel positions itself as an all-in-one HR platform designed to manage the entire lifecycle of a global employee. It combines payroll with a broad range of HR functionalities. Key services include: Global Payroll & EOR: Hire and pay workers in over 150 countries, leveraging a large network of its own legal entities. Deel HR: A built-in Human Resource Information System (HRIS) to manage employee data, time off, and reporting. Contractor Management: Tools to onboard, manage, and pay international contractors. Additional Services: Benefits administration, equipment management, and stock option grants. Key Feature Deep Dive While both platforms cover the basics, their features differ in execution and scope. Global Coverage and EOR Services Your ability to hire talent anywhere depends on your platform's global reach. Ontop provides coverage through a partner network. This model allows for flexibility and localized compliance without the overhead of maintaining entities everywhere. Deel has established its own legal entities in over 150 countries. This is a core part of their value proposition for enterprises that require direct EOR hiring across many markets. Payment Processing and Currencies Getting money to your team quickly and reliably is non-negotiable. Ontop offers multiple pay-in options for employers, including wire transfers, ACH, credit cards, and crypto. For workers, Ontop provides payments in USD to their Ontop Global Account, accessed via the Ontop Visa Platinum Card, with a focus on financial services in Latin America. Deel supports payments in over 120 currencies through methods like bank transfers and crypto. This is useful for teams spread across diverse currency zones. Compliance and Contract Management Staying compliant with local labor laws is one of the biggest challenges of global hiring. Ontop automates the creation of localized, compliant contracts that can be signed in minutes, with compliance support at all service tiers. Deel also provides localized contracts and compliance alerts, sometimes across different tiers that can add cost. Integrations and API Support Ontop provides an API and integrates with essential accounting and HR software, letting businesses build a customized HR stack. Deel offers a larger number of native integrations, reflecting its all-in-one platform approach. Pricing Models Compared Cost is a major factor when choosing between Deel alternatives for payroll. Ontop's Transparent Pricing Ontop offers a straightforward, scalable pricing model that is ideal for businesses focused on growth and cost control. Contractors: Starts at $49 per contractor, per month. EOR Employees: Starts at $499 per employee, per month. This transparent, pay-as-you-go structure makes Ontop a cost-effective solution for startups and SMBs. Deel's Tiered Pricing Deel's pricing is generally higher, reflecting its broader feature set. Contractors: Starts at $49 per contractor, per month. EOR Employees: Starts at $599 per employee, per month. While custom plans are available, the structure can be more complex and costly for companies that do not need the full suite of HR tools. What is the best platform to pay global contractors? The best platform to pay global contractors delivers the full amount, on time, in a currency the contractor controls, with compliant local contracts. Feature breadth matters less than a reliable payout and a clear price. For contractor-heavy teams that want low cost and strong worker payments, Ontop is a leading choice; enterprises needing a full HR suite may prefer Deel or Rippling. The Verdict: Why Ontop Wins for Global Payroll While Deel offers a broad HR solution, Ontop is a strong choice for businesses that need to hire, onboard, and pay global talent efficiently and affordably. Ontop focuses on the core functions of global employment. By choosing Ontop, you get: Cost-Efficiency: Lower costs for both contractor and employee management, freeing resources for growth. Simplicity and Focus: An intuitive platform that solves the most critical challenges of global payroll without unnecessary features. Compliance: Legal and tax compliance is included in all plans. Worker-Centric Tools: With built-in financial services, Ontop helps attract and retain global talent. Frequently asked questions Is Ontop a good Deel alternative? Yes, especially for startups, SMBs, and contractor-heavy teams that want lower cost and built-in worker payments. Ontop covers 150+ countries with contractor management, global payroll, and EOR. What is the cheapest way to pay international contractors? Contractor management starts at $49 per contractor per month on both Ontop and Deel; the real cost difference shows up in EOR pricing and in the FX and fees on each payout, so compare the total landed amount. Which is better for Latin America, Ontop or Deel? Ontop is built with Latin America in mind, paying workers in USD into an Ontop Global Account with the Ontop Visa Platinum Card, a strong fit for the region's contractors. Do Ontop and Deel both handle compliance? Yes. Both provide localized, compliant contracts; Ontop includes compliance support across all plans. Ready to simplify your global payroll and support your international team? Book a demo to see how Ontop compares as a Deel alternative.

title: Loving animals is not cool
body_text: My friend recently told me that he’s ditching meat. Due to my line of work, people tell me such things. Yes, once you own a plant-based business, if the content of your friends’ fridge is at least 80% not meat, you will find out about it. Generally, I am aware of most vegan dishes prepared in my vicinity. Since I’ve become a plant priest, folks confess their non-carnal sins to me on a regular basis. Anyway, what struck me as interesting was not that he is ditching meat but the way he said it. It went something like this: ‍ “Hey ... so … um... I’m vegetarian now. At least I’ll try. We’ll see. For the animals … um. I just love animals … I guess … and shit. I don’t fucking know. I guess I love ‘em. We’ll see. Maybe in a few weeks, I might crave meat again. But I don’t know, animals and shit. It’s weird, I guess. I don't know.” ‍ Animals and shit. He talked differently than usual. His demeanor had a certain elusive rhythm to it, as his words gallivanted around the true meaning behind the decision. There were unnecessary, “bro-esque” mannerisms stumbling into sentences, clearly there to diffuse the tension of truth, not to be spoken. The whole “show” reminded me of the way men hug. Idk if you noticed this, but when girls hug, they fucking hug. It’s a warm, fuzzy embrace full of presence and love. When guys hug, we tap each other’s backs. That enables us to fragment the hug, or a prolonged touch as one might call it, so as to not suddenly become gay. That can happen allegedly, and I believe it is men's greatest fear. By tapping backs we divide the “forbidden touch” into many smaller, acceptably long touches. Tapping also keeps us busy during the hug. The idea is simply “not to feel”. Yes, feeling is not cool and leads to spontaneous gayness. Why am I mentioning this? Well, I felt these “male hug” vibes in my friend’s reasoning of going meat-free. He used many redundant words, gasps, and phrases in combination with spasming body language to describe a seemingly banal decision. There he was, a grown-ass man, suddenly flexing the grammar of a teenager. He described feeling love for animals as weird. “And shit.” Why is it hard to just say “I love animals”? I don’t actually know, best I can offer is a messy thesis. The great divide Like most men, I have been raised not to cry, because boys don’t cry (and shit). Rather, we suppress. We squish emotions deep into a void within our soul. Therein lies a biological reactor, where our suppressed emotions mix with our need for validation and love, resulting in a chemical reaction that produces our endless ambition, hunger for power and wealth, fast cars, as well as our bitcoin obsession. They don’t teach you this in biology class, but this is exactly how it works. Being raised to be “a man” has created a divide within my personality. I have been detached from my natural wholeness, wherein the masculine and feminine are balanced. I’ve spent too much time and energy in pursuit of trying to be half of a person. I believe we call this phenomenon “toxic masculinity”. As a result, when ditching animal-based foods, I’ve felt trouble fusing my “masculine identity” with lifestyle changes based on “care” and “empathy”. Thanks to this culturally occurring process, my rationalizations of going plant-based have at first also been laced with rejections of care. Consequently, I started explaining going veg by telling people that “I do it for selfish reasons, health and such”, despite in reality being deeply concerned about animals, and the obvious environmental and humanitarian issues caused by animal agriculture. Care was not on the menu. That’s because when I listed animal welfare as a reason for my “veganizing”, I had shitty interactions with people. People would begin to feel uncomfortable, start fidgeting and would often start talking manically in attempts to rationalize their own meat-eating. Sometimes even arguments arose. Sadly, saying “I do it for selfish reasons” was a more acceptable reason to ditch meat than “empathy”. I’m not just talking about boys, though. Women too. Toxic masculinity is in no way limited to men. It oozes through the pores of society and we are all drenched in its bitter-sweet syrup. It manifests itself in many forms, often hidden right before our eyes. No matter how we look at it or what we call it, most of us were raised to be either A or B. And so we grow up incomplete and behave ever so strangely. Strange people in a strange world. It’s no wonder many go on to become bitter and cynical. The first-class cynical ticket One way of dealing with the strangeness of being alive today is becoming utterly cynical. It’s the easy way out. Add nihilism to the mix and you have a golden duo. The fucking Batman & Robin of bad juju. Rather than care and do something about it, you can just criticize everything and do nothing. Oui oui! It’s all rigged anyway, people are evil and dumb, and demise is imminent. I found it strange how cynically people around me reacted whenever I expressed any form of care - be it animals, environment, or people. What a fucking idiot I am for questioning the morality of killing a sentient, loving creature. Feeling like a bozo for loving animals spurred my personal growth, because I still wanted to seem cool, despite “caring and shit”. Of course I wanted to. I too need to fit in, find a mate, procreate and make new, marginally better versions of myself. I too need security offered by a strong social standing. Seeing how “caring” actually jeopardized “all that” really surprised me. So I suppressed and suppressed. As we all do. But I’ve yet to meet a person who reasonably doesn’t agree with the immorality of animal agriculture, be it carnivore or herbivore. But we use reasoning as we please. In this case, despite having a sufficient amount of reasons to stop killing 80 million animals per hour, we rather use reason to block our own emotions. Reason is the mad king in a world of emotional creatures, and so our tragicomedy never ends. We’ve cultivated a culture where “empathy” is equated with “weakness”. Cynicism is the ultimate escape. It grants us the permission to indulge in the flawed world as is while criticizing all who wish to change it for the better. There is a comfort to cynicism. It creates a feeling like there is much less to lose. Unfortunately, it leaves one with not much to gain as well. ‍ They’re not taking what little pleasure we have left In the last 100 years, as we learned more about nutrition science and how food affects our body, nutritionists and doctors started canceling certain foods. And of course, nobody ever canceled steamed peas. They came for the good stuff. They took our sugars, our fats, our bellowed gluten... and eventually, they came for our meat. Nothing matters, except this. This is where we drew the line and said: “Stop right there! Darn it, you’re not taking what little pleasure I have left in life!” Indeed, without eating meat, our lives are devoid of any joy. All that’s left is “the grind”. Might as well ditch coffee and start going to bed at 9 PM, like a fucking idiot. What’s next? Hugging my male friends without tapping backs? Shut the fuck up. Good luck, us Seeing my friend grapple with tectonic movements within his identity reminded me of my “plantening”. I went through all the stages of denial and today I stand by my feelings of “care” and “empathy”. I’m gay now, there is no other way of putting it. I also used to look at cynicism with pity, but now I have fostered an empathy towards people who suffer from it. Including myself. I realized it’s a mere symptom of a super strange society we’ve built. To remain sane among people is truly an art form. I believe everybody is giving it their best in these sub-optimal circumstances. Wow, that sounded super un-cool. Of course, not as un-cool as loving animals. Like ok, you can love dogs and cats. Also birds. As long as they are forbidden to fly. Cows however, no no no. They sit like idiots, have four stomachs, and burp greenhouse gases. ‍ ‍ I really wish it wasn’t so. I wish we’d rethink our relationship with all living creatures. But hey, is it just me, or do I sense a positive change arising in our society? I feel like we reached peak “cynical nihilism” and “toxic masculinity”, so now it’s becoming increasingly cooler to be caring, nice, and positive. Not like kumbaya positive, but you know, cool positive. I believe it’s called being “positive and shit.” PS: Today, I hug my male friends without tapping their backs. A nice little squeeze to fully feel my bros always takes the grey out of a day.

title: May 2026 Security Beat
summary: $59.52M was lost across 29 crypto incidents, down sharply from April's ~$635M. No single hack carried the month. The bigger story happened off-chain, where a self-propagating npm worm called Mini Shai-Hulud kept resurfacing in new waves through the month, ultimately spanning more than 1,000 malicious package versions across the npm ecosystem.
body_text: $59.52M was lost across 29 crypto incidents, down sharply from April's ~$635M. No single hack carried the month. Instead, the same weak points kept getting hit: cross-chain message validation, private keys, and access control. The bigger story happened off-chain, where a self-propagating npm worm called Mini Shai-Hulud kept resurfacing in new waves through the month, ultimately spanning more than 1,000 malicious package versions across the npm ecosystem. Here's the month in security 👇 ‍ Crypto: $59.52M lost across 29 incidents Category Loss Incidents Bridge / Cross-Chain ~$22.1M 3 Access Control ~$20.6M 9 Other Protocol Logic ~$5.8M 6 Key / Credential Compromise ~$10.8M 7 Price / Oracle / Flashloan ~$0.3M 4 Total $59.52M 29 Source | DeFiLlama‍ ‍ The incidents that did most of the damage Verus-Ethereum Bridge, May 17: ~$11.5M initially. Missing validation on a cross-chain import payload let an attacker forge a transfer and drain ETH, tBTC, and USDC. After bounty negotiation, the attacker reportedly returned roughly 75% (~$8.5M), which cut the net loss substantially. THORChain, May 15: $11M+. An attacker compromised functions across at least nine of THORChain's supported chains (Bitcoin, Ethereum, BSC, Base, Avalanche, Dogecoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, and XRP) and drained them simultaneously, then consolidated the proceeds into a two-address cluster. TRM Labs traced the flows within hours but has not attributed the exploit to a named actor, and the technical root cause has not been detailed publicly. It fits a long pattern: THORChain's losses since 2021 now approach $25M, and its native cross-chain swaps make it both a recurring target and a preferred laundering rail for major heists. DxSale, May 28: ~$7.3M. An ownership override attack on BSC let the attacker seize control of contracts that should have been locked down, then drain them. The purest "trusted access" failure of the month: nothing was forged or guessed, the attacker simply took over the owner role the contracts were built to trust. Source | DeFiLlama , TRM Labs ‍ Mini Shai-Hulud: the month's biggest supply chain story Mini Shai-Hulud is a self-propagating npm worm that runs at install time, steals developer and CI/CD credentials (GitHub and npm tokens, OIDC tokens, AWS and Kubernetes material, Vault tokens, SSH keys), then uses that access to republish itself into more packages. It also abuses trusted publishing, minting short-lived npm tokens inside compromised CI workflows and shipping releases with valid provenance. In May, it hit in repeated waves: an early one on May 12 (373 versions across 169 packages, heavy in TanStack), then a larger one on May 19 (639 versions across 323 packages) concentrated in the @antv ecosystem, including echarts-for-react at roughly 1.1M weekly downloads. The full campaign now spans 1,000+ malicious versions across 500+ packages, almost all on npm. For web3 teams, the exposure is direct. The worm targets exactly the machines that hold RPC keys, deploy credentials, and signing secrets, and AI coding assistants that auto-update dependencies can pull a poisoned version into a build without anyone choosing it. Pin exact versions, review dependency PRs by hand, use Socket dev or Aikido tooling to identify/block the supply chain attack, and if an affected package ran in your environment, rotate every credential reachable from that machine, not just the npm token. Source | Aikido , Socket ‍ Laravel-Lang: a backdoor aimed straight at wallets On May 23, Socket and Aikido disclosed a compromise of the community-maintained Laravel-Lang project: a remote-code-execution backdoor pushed across 700+ historical versions of packages, including laravel-lang/lang and laravel-lang/attributes. These are third-party localization packages, not the official Laravel framework, but because the malicious file sat in Composer's autoload, it ran automatically on essentially every request to an affected app. What makes this one matter for web3 is the payload: a credential stealer with a dedicated crypto module. It scans for wallet files (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Monero), browser-extension data for MetaMask, Phantom, and Trust Wallet, and even desktop folders for plaintext seed.txt or recovery.txt files, alongside the usual cloud, CI/CD, and SSH secrets. If you ran an affected version, treat the host as compromised, not just exposed: rebuild from known-good images and rotate every reachable secret, wallet keys, and seed phrases first. Source | Socket , Aikido ‍ The pattern across the month Two things ran through May: Attackers logged in, they didn't break in. Stolen or abused credentials accounted for more than half of May's losses, the kind of operational and key-management failures that sit outside the smart contract itself. The supply chain is the front line. Mini Shai-Hulud is the clearest example: the code and dependencies you don't write yourself are still your responsibility. ‍ Disclaimer This report aggregates publicly reported information as of the publication date and may be revised as investigations evolve and post-mortems are released. Recommendations are general guidance. Verify against primary sources before acting on any specific claim. ‍ About This Series Quantstamp publishes the Security Beat monthly. title: Lurk Beta: The Zero-Knowledge Proof Programming Language
summary: Argument Computer Corporation accelerates verifiable computing.
body_text: Today, we are thrilled to announce the Beta Release of Lurk, marking a significant milestone in our journey to create the premier Zero-Knowledge Proof Programming Language. This post will recap Lurk’s evolution, showcase its current capabilities, and give a glimpse into its promising future. Past (Alpha) With the Lurk Alpha release, we introduced a Turing-complete programming language designed for zero-knowledge proofs. It allowed developers to escape the confines of manually written circuits and embrace a high-level, expressive alternative. Central to Alpha was a universal verifier, capable of handling any computation expressible in Lurk’s language. This version laid the foundation for what Lurk is today, providing a robust, audited platform for early adopters. Present (Beta) Correctness In the Beta version, we have significantly enhanced the correctness of Lurk’s reduction circuit by transitioning from hand-written circuits to procedurally generated ones. This advancement is made possible through our Lurk Evaluation Model (LEM) DSL, which also facilitates the implementation of the Lurk reduction step . Customization Lurk Beta introduces Coprocessors, a major leap in customization. These allow for seamless integration of domain-specific instructions, enhancing program expressiveness and efficiency, especially in cryptographic functions. Additionally, with Circom Scotia, integrating Lurk-compatible Circom circuits into your projects has never been easier. Custom instructions are now possible through Coprocessors , enabling applications to define and implement domain-specific instructions that integrate as seamlessly as Lurk’s built-in operators. User-defined Coprocessor circuits facilitate efficient proofs for a variety of functions, particularly cryptographic ones . With Circom Scotia , defining Lurk-compatible circuits in Circom becomes straightforward, and Lurk’s support for Circom Coprocessors enhances this integration. Performance The Beta release transforms Lurk’s performance profile. While in an IVC proof, the addition of coprocessors to the Lurk evaluation circuit could bloat the cost of every folding step, with the integration of SuperNova, this is no longer a concern. Our hybrid model provides a balance between general-purpose programming and optimized arithmetic circuits, ensuring optimal performance. The NIVC support in Lurk Beta ensures that the cost of external circuits is only incurred during actual use, effectively eliminating the performance penalty of Lurk Alpha’s single universal circuit. The hybrid performance model equips Lurk with the versatility of a fully general, expressive, data-centric programming language, combined with the efficiency of custom arithmetic circuits authored in Circom or Bellpepper. Ecosystem and Stack Lurk Beta benefits from the full-stack support of Lurk Lab for the proving pipeline. Our commitment to open-source, community-focused projects enhances the agility and responsiveness of our stack, allowing us to quickly adapt and innovate in response to the needs of the ZK and Folding communities. Lurk is designed to be blockchain-friendly, particularly for efficient verificationperformance on Ethereum. This is evident in its development of low-level components, such as the switch from Pasta to Bn256/Grumpkin curve cycle, enabling the use of Ethereum precompiles for on-chain verification. Arecibo Our friendly fork of Nova, Arecibo , plays a crucial role in our ecosystem. Detailed in yesterday’s blog post , Arecibo serves as an incubator for new ideas, allowing for API finalization and design reviews, as seen with the adoption and refinement of SuperNova . Bellpepper Bellpepper , a fork of Bellperson , focuses on providing a common library for specifying arithmetic circuits, underpinning Neptune, Arecibo/Nova, and Lurk itself. Its development emphasizes broad utility, as seen in Bellpepper’s Community-Maintained Cryptographic Gadgets Library . Neptune We continue to maintain and optimize Neptune , our Poseidon hashing and circuit library, leveraging Bellpepper’s advancements for significant improvements in synthesis time. Taking advantage of Bellpepper’s optimized witness-generation circuit, we implemented optimized witness-generation . This led to optimizations yielding 16x improvements in synthesis time . Future (1.0 and beyond) Lurk 1.0 ZeroMorph Integration : We’re integrating the ZeroMorph polynomial commitment scheme into Nova, promising faster verification processes. This integration, coupled with the CycleFold protocol , aims to produce smaller proofs and enhanced efficiency. LEM-Driven Development : LEM ensures the equivalence between the Lurk interpreter’s description and the enforcing circuit. It enables faster iterations on algorithmic improvements to reduce Lurk iterations (e.g., more efficient data structures) and the introduction of new language features beyond Alpha’s core (e.g., exception management, or new operators such as the list and apply operators from Common Lisp, and type assertions ) Parallel Folding : Inspired by Privacy Scaling Explorations’ ParaNova and Lagrange’s contributions, we’re exploring parallel folding to integrate these insights into Lurk. This includes work on Arecibo Paranova Integration and expanding to encompass Binary PCD . Concurrent Lurk (Lurk 2.0?) We are envisioning an Actor Model Concurrency for Lurk, enabling proofs of truly distributed computation and opening new horizons in zero-knowledge proof programming.

title: What Is a Container, Really? Five Years of GPU Infrastructure
summary: Five years of GPU infrastructure at Beam — from ECS and Knative cold starts to a custom container runtime, FUSE lazy-loading, and a trustless binary.
body_text: We've been doing this for a while. We started the company with the idea that it should be dead simple to deploy models – an AWS Lambda for GPUs. Since then, we've faced almost every infrastructure problem there is. Let me start at the beginning. Starting naively on ECS When we started building, we were building a cloud IDE, sort of like Replit for ML. For the first year or so, we were focused on making it easy to fork and launch machine learning models from your browser, so we invested heavily in the front end. The backend left a lot to be desired. I'd used ECS before for data pipelines and was familiar with it, so we started there. Our ECS architecture was naive. We'd generate a Dockerfile for each user, bundle their code into it, and spawn an ECS container that embedded a small webserver alongside their code. It was simple, and it kind of worked. This is the demo we raised our pre-seed round with. As soon as we started running real models, it stopped working. We kept ECS workers running, so it wasn't truly serverless. We just dynamically loaded and unloaded user code on demand to fake it. As we began onboarding our first users into production, we came across the core problem: cold start. That was the thing we'd be fighting (in one form or another) for years. Knative scaling woes The cold-start problem pushed us toward a second version of the system, and toward Kubernetes. I tend to reach for the easiest available thing, so I went looking for something off-the-shelf, truly scale-to-zero, and Kubernetes-native. Knative fit, so we built V2 on top of it: a custom operator, CRDs for our deployment resources, and internally roughly the same server as before: dynamically loaded user code, and a separate image tag per deployment version. Knative plus Kubernetes was a real improvement. It let us lean on the K8s ecosystem for things like proactive image caching, just warming the disk on nodes with a tool called kube-fledged. And around this time we did something we should have done much earlier: we instrumented the system end to end. We'd been so focused on getting something that worked that we knew when things were slow but not why. So we started shipping metrics. The data confirmed our suspicions and ranked them. Three things were slow: starting GPU nodes, loading large images stuffed with CUDA dependencies, and loading model weights into RAM and then into VRAM. By far the biggest was starting the GPU node itself. We kept an overprovisioned warm pool to hide it, but that was expensive, so we spent real effort optimizing node bootstrap. That turned out to be wasted work. We were optimizing at the wrong layer. (In today's market it makes even less sense to optimize there: GPUs are scarce enough that you cling to whatever capacity you can get. But that's another story.) I remember the moment when this became a hair-on-fire problem for us. One of our first production users was running a large inference workload, and at that stage we didn't even have a queuing system for inference. The way we "scaled" their workload was to add containers via Knative, with load balancing at the Kubernetes service level, in front of what was (at that point) just a FastAPI server. It was trash, and it failed in the most visible way possible. We'd set up a shared Slack channel with the customer, and they'd wired a hook to post a message every single time their pipeline threw an error. So we sat there getting bombarded with error messages, over and over. We tuned every Knative setting there was. We forked it. We changed the autoscaling parameters, rewrote the proxy behavior, tried a month of small tweaks. None of it worked, and watching exactly where it broke is what produced the diagnosis the whole rest of this story follows from. The problem was twofold. First, Knative's autoscaling and request buffering were built for web traffic – they can't handle APIs where each request carries this much latency. You cannot scale an inference pipeline the way you scale a CRUD service; you're operating under false pretenses, and it will not work. Second, even with perfect request buffering, container start and model load time were high enough that it wouldn't matter — you can't buffer your way out of not being able to start the container fast enough. So there were two problems, not one. How fast can you start a container, and how do you autoscale and proxy requests for workloads that don't behave like web requests. We had to solve both. (For what it's worth, the Knative fork was a short blip, about a month. Nobody really pushed back on the decision to leave it, mostly because nobody outside the company knew what we were doing internally.) What is a container, really? The second problem (request routing, queuing, proxying) we solved by building our own control plane and leaving the Knative world entirely. But the first problem sent us somewhere stranger. We started asking a genuinely basic question: what is a container, really? And why are we pulling an entire image when we only ever touch a fraction of the files inside it? A container, it turns out, is not much. It's a process group and a set of namespaces in Linux with a different root filesystem, and that root filesystem is just stacked layers composed through an overlay filesystem. Once you actually internalize that, you realize that if the container only reads a subset of the files, you don't need the whole image present to start it. You can lazy-load the contents on demand. To do that you need to sit underneath the filesystem, which means FUSE. So we built two things. First, our own container runtime in Go that could spin up containers directly from a root filesystem. Essentially what Docker does under the hood. Second, a custom image format that let us lazy-load contents through that filesystem. This was our first real step toward mature infrastructure, and we bundled it, along with a new control plane that owned the full container lifecycle, into what we called Beam V1. We also built a scheduler that sat above Kubernetes. We still relied on the Kubernetes scheduler for the workers that actually spawn containers, but our scheduler let us write custom logic around the attributes a given container needed to run. By this point the company itself had shifted: we'd moved off the browser IDE and become a Python SDK. Besides our developer experience, there was nothing flashy in the product anymore. It was entirely the system beneath the surface that mattered. Performance was the product. Why FUSE? FUSE looks like a strange place to spend your engineering budget until you see what it buys you. The key fact is that loading a model image touches a very uneven slice of the files. Some are enormous. A CUDA library can be gigabytes. But a huge amount of what gets read is tiny: the long tail of __init__ files, .pyc files, the small Python files that make up an inference script. And a lot of the image never gets read at all, even though you're still decompressing and mounting it. FUSE gave us three things. It made the access pattern visible. Because FUSE intercepts every read, open, and lookup, mounting a root filesystem through it lets you see exactly which files a container touches as it runs. We could add hooks to record precisely what was required to load a given image. It made caching programmatic. That same per-lookup hook meant we could proactively cache exactly the content that got accessed, however we wanted: on local disk, or (where we eventually landed) in a distributed networked cache. It decoupled storage from compute. FUSE is just an interface; what it does underneath is arbitrary. The image contents don't have to live on the machine running the container. You could serve a layer from another node entirely. If you're spinning up fifty containers across a cluster, one node can serve the image instead of duplicating that storage on every server. The result was subsecond container starts without the image ever living on the box running the container. And because the cache was content-addressed (keyed on the hash of the content) it produced a network effect. The more users we had, the better it got for everyone: two users pulling the same CUDA library or the same base image hit a cache the other had already warmed. V1 to V2: the long tail Our first filesystem compressed everything down into a single layer. You could lazy-load individual files out of it and never store the layers themselves in the cache. It was a good enough implementation for about a year. But it had a structural flaw: by collapsing everything into one layer, you lose the cross-user network effect at build time, because you can no longer match on shared layer hashes, and most people are building on the same handful of base images. So we built V2: a system that indexes within individual layers. Given an arbitrary file path, we can determine which layer it lives in based on how the layers stack, and (because of the index) the exact byte offset of that content in the decompressed layer. That means you don't build the overlay filesystem at all. You don't download every layer and assemble it. You go straight to the decompressed layer and pull the file out of the cache. It's truly the best of both worlds: per-file seeking and cross-user caching. It also fixed builds. Compress everything to one layer and you rebuild the whole thing on every change; index individual layers and you get Docker's normal behavior back, where only layers above the lowest change rebuild, so builds get faster and multiple users share cached contents. That's why it's V2. The interesting thing about going from V1-to-V2 is what it did and didn't improve. p50 latency stayed about the same. p90 probably did too. The entire gain was in p95 and p99. More cache hits means more requests that skip the slow path. We'd already gotten a taste of how fast the best case could be once V1 worked; V2 was about making that speed the common case, for more users, most of the time. The trustless binary We run across a lot of different cloud providers, chasing cheaper and more available hardware, and the system that got us this far was annoying to deploy. We had Kubernetes installed on every GPU node, with daemonsets orchestrating the caching layer, credential management, and the rest, all rolled out with tools like Flux. It worked, but every new pool of hardware made it more painful. We wanted something we could stand up with one dumb command. As we went through SOC 2, the auditors' questions forced us to address questions we hadn't really asked ourselves: what does a worker actually need to know to run a workload, and where are the boundaries of the system? Once we looked, the gaps were everywhere. The worker had a direct connection to Redis, which meant it needed Redis credentials. It had direct database access to update things in Postgres. Every time we changed anything, the service boundary turned out to be in the wrong place. You really don't want a remote machine (possibly on someone else's cloud) storing your Redis credentials. We closed the gaps, one by one. Today, a node comes up with a temporary token that authenticates it to the control plane, spins up its own copy of the distributed cache and its own worker, and mounts the image filesystems to run containers. There are no daemonsets on remote nodes. No Kubernetes on remote nodes. No saved credentials. If a remote node is compromised, it can't touch other users or other nodes. There are fewer dependencies, fewer services to see, fewer credentials to store, and fewer networking decisions to make. We didn't set out to build something you could run anywhere. We set out to make our own lives less annoying and our security boundary defensible. But the benefit of shrinking our footprint this small is that people mostly interact with our system as a binary you can drop onto any machine and run. Which, if you go back to the very beginning, is actually quite close to what we wanted to build in the first place. Something dead simple, for GPUs, that runs wherever and whenever you need it. If you're interested in seeing the infra in action, you can get started for free right away . And if the sorts of problems in this article excite you, we're hiring .

title: Leadership that starts with people at VPI Spokane: Meet Ken Harrison
summary: See how a people-first leadership approach is empowering teams to drive operational excellence and continuous improvement at our VPI Quality Windows facility.
body_text: Share this page Email Print Subscribe 04/27/2026 Leadership that starts with people at VPI Spokane: Meet Ken Harrison See how a people-first leadership approach is empowering teams to drive operational excellence and continuous improvement at our VPI Quality Windows facility. As Plant Manager at JELD-WEN’s VPI Quality Windows Spokane facility, Ken Harrison leads with a clear belief that strong operations start with strong people. From safety and quality to innovation and sustainability, Ken is focused on fostering a plant culture where accountability, trust and continuous improvement drive long ‑ term success. Leading a safety-first culture through clarity and trust For Ken, safety on the plant floor goes far beyond rules and checklists; it’s a reflection of shared values and leadership behavior. “Safety has to start with leadership and show up in the decisions we make every day,” Ken says. At its core, safety is about empowering employees to make the right choices, even when no one is watching. During challenging production periods or tight deadlines, Ken’s leadership approach is grounded in clarity and support. He prioritizes removing obstacles, staying close to the work and maintaining short, frequent check ‑ ins on the plant floor. Clear expectations and a shared definition of success help teams stay focused under pressure, while celebrating small wins helps build momentum, morale, and a strong safety culture. Developing the next generation of leaders Ken is intentional about identifying and developing future leaders within his plant. He looks for individuals who remain composed under pressure, demonstrate an ownership mindset, and earn trust through consistent performance. “Strong leaders don’t need to be micromanaged,” Ken says. “They’re the ones you can trust to handle critical priorities, bring stability to the team, and do the right thing when it matters most.” By fostering these qualities, Ken is helping build a strong leadership pipeline that supports long-term operational stability and growth. Improving efficiency, quality, and long‑term performance While still relatively new to the organization, Ken is already helping guide VPI Spokane through a significant project scheduled for completion in June. The initiative is expected to deliver meaningful efficiency improvements and reduce warranty claims, supporting operational excellence and customer satisfaction. Quality, in Ken’s view, is non ‑ negotiable. He believes that when production demands compromise in quality, it signals an opportunity to improve the system. By prioritizing in ‑ process product and process audits instead of relying solely on final inspections, the team is working to ensure quality is built into every step of manufacturing. What matters most Ultimately, what motivates Ken most is developing people. “Helping team members grow and reach their potential is the most rewarding part of the job,” he says. “I was fortunate to have great mentors early in my career, and I see this as a way to pay that forward.” Supported by a dedicated team across operations, EH&S, supply chain, and quality, Ken continues to balance the needs of employees, customers, and the business, living JELD-WEN’s values every day.
